title: Notitia means evident distinct knowledge; rude confused apprehension suffices for faith
source_text: XXV. Verum ut hac in parte mens eorum percipiatur, observandum est illos, dum negant fidem esse notitiam, & asserunt fidem opponi quodammodo scientiae & intelligentiae, illos, inquam, per notitiam, scientiam & intelligentiam designare cognitionem aliquam evidentem, aut saltem distinctam atque accuratam. Itaque per hoc significatum volunt, primo fideles evidenter non cognoscere mysteria quae credunt, nec iis assentiri propter aliquam, quam in ipsis percipiant, evidentiam, sed solummodo propter authoritatem Dei testimonium ipsis in Verbo perhibentis. Deinde quoque ad fidem necessario non requiri distinctam & perspicuam apprehensionem eorum quae creduntur; qualis est in iis qui fidei mysteria aliis explicare, argumentis probare, & adversus contradicentes tueri & vindicare possunt: sed ad fidem concipiendam sufficere rudem quandam & confusam apprehensionem mysteriorum divinorum, qualis est in idiotis, qui credunt mysteria Trinitatis & Incarnationis, etiamsi mysteria illa distincte & accurate nec intelligant ipsi, nec aliis explicare possint. Ac tandem qualicunque mysteriorum divinorum conceptio & apprehensio in credente reperiatur, fidem in apprehensione illa proprie non consistere, sed potius in assensu quem mysteriis istis praebet ille qui credit.
pass_a_gloss: But so that their mind in this part may be perceived, it must be observed that when they deny faith is notitia and assert that faith is somehow opposed to knowledge and understanding, they designate by notitia, scientia, and intelligentia some evident cognition, or at least distinct and accurate cognition. By this they mean, first, that the faithful do not know the mysteries they believe with evidence, nor assent to them because of some evidence they perceive in the things themselves, but only because of the authority of God bearing them testimony in the Word. Second, that a distinct and clear apprehension of what is believed is not necessarily required for faith, such as belongs to those who can explain the mysteries of faith to others, prove them with arguments, and defend them against contradictors; but that for conceiving faith a rude and confused apprehension of the divine mysteries suffices, such as is in the unlearned who believe the mysteries of the Trinity and Incarnation even though they neither understand those mysteries distinctly and accurately themselves nor can explain them to others. And finally, whatever conception and apprehension of the divine mysteries is found in the believer, faith does not properly consist in that apprehension, but rather in the assent which the one who believes gives to those mysteries.
pass_b_english: When Romans deny faith is notitia and oppose faith to scientia, they mean evident or at least distinct accurate cognition, not every grasp of the object.

Believers need not see evidence in the mysteries themselves, nor have the clear grasp of teachers who explain and defend them; a rude confused apprehension, as in the unlearned who believe Trinity and Incarnation, is enough, and faith properly sits in assent rather than in that apprehension.
